title: Chapter 110 — Queequeg in His Coffin
paragraphs: When they searched, they found that the casks most recently lowered into the hold were perfectly sound, and that the leak must be farther off. So, since the weather was calm, they broke out deeper and deeper, disturbing the slumbers of the huge ground-tier butts and sending those gigantic moles up from that black midnight into the daylight above. They went so deep, and the lowest puncheons looked so ancient, corroded and weedy, that you almost expected to find next some moldy cornerstone cask containing coins of Captain Noah, along with copies of the posted placards that vainly warned the infatuated old world about the flood. Tierce after tierce of water, and bread, and beef, too, and shooks of staves (bundled staves for making casks), and iron bundles of hoops, were hoisted out, until at last the piled decks were hard to get about on; and the hollow hull echoed underfoot, as if you were treading over empty catacombs, and reeled and rolled in the sea like a demijohn with nothing but air for freight. The ship was as top-heavy as a dinnerless student with all of Aristotle in his head. It was just as well that the Typhoons did not visit them then.
Now it was at this time that my poor pagan companion and close bosom friend, Queequeg, was seized with a fever, which brought him near to his endless end.

Let it be said that in this vocation of whaling, sinecures are unknown; dignity and danger go hand in hand; until you become captain, the higher you rise, the harder you toil. So it was with poor Queequeg, who, as harpooner, must not only face all the rage of the living whale, but — as we have seen elsewhere — mount his dead back in a rolling sea; and finally go down into the gloom of the hold and, sweating bitterly all day in that underground confinement, resolutely manhandle the clumsiest casks and see to their stowage. In short, among whalemen, the harpooners are the holders, as they are called.

Poor Queequeg! When the ship was about half disemboweled, you should have stooped over the hatchway and peered down at him there, where, stripped to his woolen drawers, the tattooed savage was crawling about amid that dampness and slime like a green spotted lizard at the bottom of a well. And a well, or an icehouse, it somehow proved to be for him, poor pagan; for there, strange to say, for all the heat of his sweating, he caught a terrible chill which turned into a fever, and at last, after some days' suffering, laid him in his hammock, close to the very sill of the door of death. How he wasted and wasted away in those few long, lingering days, until there seemed little left of him but his frame and his tattooing. But as everything else in him thinned, and his cheekbones grew sharper, his eyes nevertheless seemed to grow fuller and fuller; they took on a strange softness of luster, and looked out at you mildly but deeply from his sickness, a wondrous testimony to that immortal health in him which could not die or be weakened. And like circles on the water, which expand as they grow fainter, his eyes seemed rounding and rounding, like the rings of Eternity. An awe that cannot be named would steal over you as you sat beside this waning savage and saw things in his face as strange as any seen by those who stood by when Zoroaster died. For whatever is truly wondrous and fearful in man has never yet been put into words or books. And the approach of Death, which levels all alike, impresses all alike with a last revelation, which only an author returned from the dead could adequately tell. So that — let us say it again — no dying Chaldee or Greek had higher and holier thoughts than those whose mysterious shadows you saw creeping over the face of poor Queequeg, as he lay quietly in his swaying hammock, and the rolling sea seemed to be gently rocking him to his final rest, and the ocean's invisible flood-tide lifted him higher and higher toward his destined heaven.

Every man in the crew gave him up for lost; and as for Queequeg himself, what he thought of his condition was forcibly shown by a curious favor he asked. He called one of the men to him in the gray morning watch, just as day was breaking, and, taking his hand, said that while in Nantucket he had happened to see certain little canoes of dark wood, like the rich war-wood of his native island; and on inquiring, he had learned that all whalemen who died in Nantucket were laid in those same dark canoes, and that the idea of being laid out that way had greatly pleased him. For it was not unlike the custom of his own people, who, after embalming a dead warrior, stretched him out in his canoe and so left him to be floated away to the starry archipelagoes; for not only do they believe that the stars are islands, but that far beyond all visible horizons their own mild, uncontinented seas flow together with the blue heavens, and so form the white breakers of the Milky Way. He added that he shuddered at the thought of being buried in his hammock, according to the usual custom at sea, tossed like something vile to the death-devouring sharks. No: he wanted a canoe like those of Nantucket, all the more congenial to him as a whaleman because, like a whaleboat, these coffin-canoes had no keel — though that meant uncertain steering, and a great deal of leeway down the dim ages.

Now, when this strange circumstance was made known aft, the carpenter was at once ordered to do Queequeg's bidding, whatever it might involve. There was some heathenish, coffin-colored old lumber aboard, which, on a long voyage some time before, had been cut from the aboriginal groves of the Lackaday islands, and it was recommended that the coffin be made from these dark planks. No sooner had the carpenter been told of the order than he took his rule and, with all the indifferent promptness of his character, went straight into the forecastle and took Queequeg's measure with great accuracy, regularly marking Queequeg's person with chalk as he shifted the rule.
"Ah! poor fellow! he'll have to die now," exclaimed the Long Island sailor.

Going to his vise-bench, the carpenter, for convenience' sake and general reference, now measured off on it, by transfer, the exact length the coffin was to be, and then made the record permanent by cutting two notches at its ends. This done, he marshaled the planks and his tools, and set to work.
Once the last nail had been driven in and the lid properly planed and fitted, he swung the coffin easily onto his shoulder and carried it forward, asking whether they were ready for it up there yet.

Queequeg overheard the indignant, half-joking shouts with which the men on deck started to chase the coffin away, and, to everyone's dismay, he ordered it brought to him at once. There was no refusing him, since some dying men are the most tyrannical of all mortals; and surely, since they will soon trouble us so little forever after, the poor fellows ought to be humored.

Leaning out of his hammock, Queequeg studied the coffin closely for a long time. Then he asked for his harpoon, had the wooden shaft taken out of it, and had the iron part laid in the coffin together with one of the paddles from his boat. Next, again at his own request, biscuits were lined up around the inside walls; a flask of fresh water was set at the head, and at the foot a small bag of woody earth scraped up from the hold. A piece of sailcloth was rolled up for a pillow, and then Queequeg begged to be lifted into his final bed so that he could test how comfortable it was, if it was comfortable at all. He lay still for a few minutes, then told someone to go to his bag and bring out his little god, Yojo. Then he crossed his arms on his chest with Yojo between them and asked for the coffin lid (he called it the hatch) to be put over him. The head section folded back on a leather hinge, and there lay Queequeg in his coffin with hardly anything showing but his calm face. "Rarmai" (it will do; it is easy), he murmured at last, and signaled to be put back in his hammock.
But before this was done, Pip, who had been slyly hovering nearby all this while, came close to him where he lay and, with soft sobs, took him by the hand, holding his tambourine in the other.

"Poor rover! Will you never be done with all this weary roving? Where are you going now? But if the currents carry you to those sweet Antilles where the beaches are beaten only by water-lilies, will you do one little errand for me? Seek out one Pip, who's been missing a long time now: I think he's in those far Antilles. If you find him, then comfort him, for he must be very sad; for look! he's left his tambourine behind — I found it. Rig-a-dig, dig, dig! Now, Queequeg, die; and I'll beat you your dying march."

"I have heard," murmured Starbuck, gazing down the scuttle, "that in violent fevers men wholly without learning have talked in ancient languages; and that when the mystery is looked into, it always turns out that in their wholly forgotten childhood those ancient languages had really been spoken in their hearing by some lofty scholars. So, in my fond faith, poor Pip, in this strange sweetness of his lunacy, brings heavenly vouchers of all our heavenly homes. Where did he learn that, if not there? — Listen! He's speaking again: but more wildly now."

"Form up two by two! Let's make a General of him! Ho, where's his harpoon? Lay it across here. — Rig-a-dig, dig, dig! Hurrah! Oh, for a gamecock now to sit on his head and crow! Queequeg dies game! — mind you that; Queequeg dies game! — take good note of that; Queequeg dies game! I say; game, game, game! But base little Pip, he died a coward; died all a-shiver — shame on Pip! Listen; if you find Pip, tell all the Antilles he's a runaway; a coward, a coward, a coward! Tell them he jumped from a whaleboat! I'd never beat my tambourine over base Pip, and hail him General, if he were dying here once more. No, no! Shame on all cowards — shame on them! Let them go drown like Pip, who jumped from a whaleboat. Shame! Shame!"
Through all of this Queequeg lay with his eyes shut, as if he were dreaming. Pip was led away, and the sick man was put back in his hammock.

But now that he had apparently made every preparation for death, now that his coffin had proved a good fit, Queequeg suddenly rallied; soon there seemed no need for the carpenter's box. And then, when some expressed their delighted surprise, he said, in substance, that the cause of his sudden recovery was this: at a critical moment he had just remembered a little duty ashore that he was leaving undone, and so had changed his mind about dying; he could not die yet, he declared. They asked him, then, whether living or dying was a matter of his own sovereign will and pleasure. He answered, certainly. In a word, it was Queequeg's notion that if a man made up his mind to live, mere sickness could not kill him: nothing but a whale, or a gale, or some violent, ungovernable, unintelligent destroyer of that sort.

Now, there is this noteworthy difference between savage and civilized: while a sick civilized man may take six months to recover, generally speaking a sick savage is almost half-well again in a day. So in good time my Queequeg gained strength; and at length, after sitting on the windlass for a few idle days (but eating with a vigorous appetite), he suddenly leaped to his feet, threw out his arms and legs, gave himself a good stretch, yawned a little, and then, springing into the head of his hoisted boat and poising a harpoon, declared himself fit for a fight.

With a wild whimsicality, he now used his coffin as a sea-chest; and emptying his canvas bag of clothes into it, he set them in order there. He spent many spare hours carving the lid with all kinds of grotesque figures and drawings; and it seemed that in this way he was trying, in his rough fashion, to copy parts of the twisted tattooing on his body. And this tattooing had been the work of a departed prophet and seer of his island, who, by those hieroglyphic marks, had written out on his body a complete theory of the heavens and the earth, and a mystical treatise on the art of attaining truth; so that Queequeg in his own proper person was a riddle to unfold, a wondrous work in one volume, but one whose mysteries not even he himself could read, though his own living heart beat against them; and these mysteries were therefore destined in the end to molder away with the living parchment on which they were inscribed, and so remain unsolved to the last. And it must have been this thought that prompted Ahab's wild exclamation when, one morning, he turned away from surveying poor Queequeg — "Oh, devilish tantalization of the gods!"
